Outlook
Global growth is expected to remain moderate as geopolitical 
developments, trade disruptions and tighter financial conditions 
weigh on economic activity. The impact is expected to remain 
uneven across economies, with energy importers and markets 
more exposed to global trade facing greater pressures. At 
the same time, economies integrated into technology value 
chains are benefiting from stronger investment in AI-related 
infrastructure and applications, providing an offset to some of 
the broader weakness.
The disinflation process has also stalled. Global headline 
inflation is projected to rise from 4.1% in CY 2025 to 4.7% in 
CY 2026, before easing to 3.9% in CY 2027. Higher energy and 
commodity prices have contributed to renewed price pressures, 
while the continued reconfiguration of global supply chains is 
adding to cost uncertainty. Global trade growth is projected to 
moderate from 5.0% in CY 2025 to 3.5% in CY 2026, before 
recovering to 4.3% in CY 2027.
Growth across major economies remains differentiated. The 
United States is projected to grow by 2.3% in CY 2026, while 
the Euro Area is expected to expand by only 0.9%. Emerging 
market and developing economies are projected to grow by 
3.8%, with Emerging and Developing Asia continuing to record 
comparatively stronger growth at 5.0%.Management Discussion and Analysis
Geopolitical developments remain a key source of uncertainty. 
A prolonged or renewed escalation of conflict could place 
further pressure on energy prices, transportation networks 
and supply chains, while deeper trade fragmentation could 
constrain global investment and commerce. Financial market 
repricing, elevated debt levels and limited policy buffers add to 
the vulnerabilities.
The outlook also retains potential upside from stronger 
productivity gains, an easing of trade restrictions and 
stabilisation in energy markets. Overall, the global economy 
is entering the next phase with moderate growth, elevated 
geopolitical uncertainty and continued shifts in trade and 
supply-chain relationships.
Indian Economic Overview
India remained one of the fastest-growing major economies 
in FY 2025-26, with real GDP growth accelerating to 7.7%, 
compared with 7.1% in FY 2024-25. Real GVA grew by 7.9% 
during FY 2025-26, reflecting sustained momentum across 
economic activity through the year.
Growth remained broad-based, supported by agriculture and 
allied activities, manufacturing, construction and services. 
Domestic demand continued to provide a strong foundation, 
while investment activity was supported by sustained public 
capital expenditure and infrastructure development. The 
external sector also remained supportive, with exports of 
goods and services increasing by 9.3% during FY 2025-26.
The economic environment, however, remained influenced 
by developments in global markets. Geopolitical tensions, 
disruptions to international routes and supply chains, higher 
energy prices and currency movements created pockets of 
cost and operational pressure. During FY 2025-26, airspace 
closures across West Asia forced long-haul carriers into 
extended flight paths, resulting in heightened fuel consumption 
and localized jet fuel supply constraints. Concurrently, isolated 
domestic fuel shortages and surges in global crude import 
costs squeezed transportation and industrial supply chains, 
while movements in the Rupee against major international 
currencies further elevated import expenses.
India’s underlying economic fundamentals remained 
supportive despite these external pressures. Continued 
infrastructure investment and improvements in transport 
and digital connectivity strengthened the foundations for 
economic activity, while domestic consumption and services 
continued to provide important support to growth. The Union 
Budget 2026-27 further reinforced the focus on infrastructure-
led growth, with public capital expenditure increased to 12.2 
trillion, up from 11.1 trillion in FY 2025-26.
189
Outlook
Looking ahead, the IMF projects India’s real GDP growth at 
6.4% in FY 2026-27, followed by 6.7% in FY 2027-28. While this 
represents a moderation from the 7.7% recorded in FY 2025-
26, India is expected to remain among the faster-growing 
major economies. Domestic demand, investment and services 
activity are expected to remain important drivers, while the 
external environment will continue to influence the pace and 
composition of growth.
The outlook will remain shaped by the interaction between 
India’s strong domestic fundamentals and external 
developments. Geopolitical conditions, energy prices, global 
trade flows and currency movements remain important 
variables, while continued investment in infrastructure, 
connectivity and productive capacity provides a foundation for 
sustained economic expansion.
Industry Overview
Foreign Exchange Industry Review
The Indian foreign exchange industry continued to expand, 
supported by rising cross-border trade, FDI flows, NRI 
remittances, corporate globalisation and India’s growing 
integration with global capital markets.
The market is also undergoing structural transformation. Digital 
forex platforms, mobile-first services, electronic execution and 
automated KYC and compliance are improving accessibility 
and transaction efficiency, while growing corporate adoption 
of currency swaps, forwards and options is strengthening 
demand for sophisticated hedging solutions. Cross-border 
trade and investment, corporate treasury requirements, 
international travel, overseas education and remittances 
remain important sources of demand for foreign exchange 
and cross-border payment services. In India, however, outward 
remittance flows under the Reserve Bank of India’s Liberalised 
Remittance Scheme (LRS) moderated during FY 2025-26. Total 
LRS remittances stood at US$28.98 billion, compared with 
US$29.56 billion in FY 2024-25, representing a 2% decline year-
on-year. Travel-related remittances declined 3% to US$16.44 
billion, maintenance of close relatives declined 5% to US$3.54 
billion, and remittances for studies abroad declined 21% to 
US$2.31 billion. The ‘Others’ category, however, increased 12% 
to US$6.69 billion.

India’s strong remittance flows provide an additional structural 
support to the market. India remained the world’s largest recipient of remittances, while rising NRI inflows continue 
to contribute to foreign exchange liquidity. The RBI also

deposits.
The RBI’s continued easing and clarification of foreign 
exchange regulations is supporting this evolution. Under the 
Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), resident individuals can 
remit up to US$250,000 per financial year for permitted current 
and capital account transactions.
Together, these developments are contributing to a more flexible 
and accessible foreign exchange ecosystem. Increasing cross-
border activity, strong remittance flows, greater corporate 
use of hedging instruments and a more liberalised regulatory 
framework are expected to support continued expansion of 
India’s forex market, while technology-led platforms continue 
to improve transaction efficiency and accessibility.
Global Travel and Tourism Industry
The global Travel & Tourism industry continued its expansion 
in CY 2025, with international tourist arrivals reaching  
~1.54 billion. The sector contributed around US$11.6 trillion 
to the global economy, equivalent to 9.8% of global GDP , 
and supported ~366 million jobs. Travel & Tourism grew 
faster than the wider global economy, supported by resilient 
leisure demand, recovering international mobility, improving 
connectivity and continued investment across the tourism 
ecosystem.
The momentum continued into the beginning of 2026, although 
regional performance became increasingly differentiated. 
International tourist arrivals were 2% higher year-on-year in 
Q1 2026, with Europe and Africa each recording 4% growth, 
Asia-Pacific 3% and the Americas 2%. The Middle East was 
the exception, with arrivals declining 14% during the quarter 
amid the escalation of conflict and associated disruptions to 
air travel.
The scale of disruption in the Middle East is significant for 
international travel because of the region’s role as a major 
aviation and transit hub. The region accounts for ~5% of global 
international arrivals and 14% of global international transit 
traffic. Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha and Bahrain together normally 
process around 526,000 passengers per day. According to 
WTTC, the escalating Iran conflict was already affecting 
international visitor spending across the Middle East by at least 
US$600 million per day as of March 2026. WTTC’s estimate 
was based on a pre-conflict forecast of US$207 billion in 
international visitor spending across the region for 2026.
The developments highlight the increasingly uneven nature of 
the global tourism landscape. While aggregate international 
travel demand remains positive, geopolitical events can quickly 
affect destination demand, aviation connectivity and traveller 
confidence. This is particularly relevant for travel corridors 
that serve as major connecting points between regions, where 
disruption can influence travel flows beyond the markets 
directly affected.

Outlook
The global tourism industry is expected to maintain its growth 
trajectory in CY 2026, although at a more measured and uneven 
pace. WTTC forecasts Travel & Tourism GDP to grow 3.2% 
during the year, ahead of projected global economic growth of 
2.4%. The sector is expected to contribute ~US$12 trillion to 
the global economy and support 376 million jobs, equivalent to 
around one in nine jobs globally. Over the next decade, Travel 
& Tourism GDP is projected to grow at an annual rate of 3.6%, 
compared with 2.4% for the wider economy.
Travel demand is expected to receive support from continued 
consumer interest in leisure and international travel, improving 
connectivity and the recovery of mobility across several 
markets. Major international events, including the FIFA 
World Cup 2026, are also expected to generate additional 
travel demand, particularly across host markets and their 
neighbouring destinations.
However, geopolitical and economic risks could moderate 
the pace of expansion. The conflict in the Middle East has 
disrupted energy markets and logistics, with the World Bank 
projecting Brent crude prices to average US$94 per barrel in 
2026, 36% above 2025 levels. Global inflation is also projected 
to rise to 4.0% in 2026 from 3.3% in 2025, potentially adding to 
transportation and other travel-related costs.
Trade uncertainty, climate-related disruptions and elevated 
travel costs could further influence traveller sentiment and 
spending patterns. Higher transportation costs may encourage 
greater price sensitivity, while uncertainty around air routes 
and destination accessibility could influence itinerary choices. 
Travellers may increasingly favour shorter-haul or regional 
journeys, flexible travel arrangements and destinations offering 
reliable connectivity and value.
Overall, the industry is expected to remain on a growth 
trajectory, but the distribution of this growth is likely to remain 
uneven across markets. For travel businesses, diversification 
of source markets and routes, flexibility in travel offerings and 
the ability to respond quickly to changes in connectivity, costs 
and traveller behaviour will become increasingly important in 
navigating the evolving operating environment.
Indian Travel and Tourism Industry Overview
India’s travel and tourism industry continued to expand 
during FY 2025-26, supported by resilient domestic demand, 
improving connectivity, rising discretionary spending and 
sustained investment in tourism infrastructure. The sector remained an important contributor to economic activity, 
employment and foreign exchange earnings, while supporting 
a wide ecosystem spanning transportation, accommodation, 
retail, food services, entertainment and local enterprises.
Domestic tourism remained the principal engine of growth. 
India recorded more than 4.13 billion domestic tourist visits 
in 2025, up from around 2.94 billion in 2024, reflecting the 
continued expansion of travel beyond metropolitan centres. 
Rising participation from Tier II and Tier III cities, improved 
road and regional air connectivity, and greater preference for 
short-haul and experience-led travel supported demand.
The demand profile is also becoming more diverse. Travellers 
are increasingly seeking experiential, spiritual, cultural, 
wellness and adventure-led journeys, alongside conventional 
leisure travel. Spiritual and pilgrimage tourism received 
significant impetus from events such as Maha Kumbh 2025, 
while improved destination infrastructure and connectivity are 
supporting the development of heritage, wildlife, eco-tourism 
and rural destinations. MICE, cruise and other niche segments 
are further broadening India’s tourism proposition. India 
recorded 20.57 million International Tourist Arrivals in 2024, 
14.85% above the 2019 level, while Foreign Tourist Arrivals 
stood at 9.95 million. Foreign Exchange Earnings from tourism 
reached `2.93 lakh crore in 2024. In 2025, FTAs increased 
further to 9.15 million, indicating continued recovery in inbound 
travel, although international demand remains below India’s 
longer-term potential.
India’s opportunity extends beyond increasing visitor numbers 
to capturing greater international visitor spending. WTTC 
estimates that international visitors spend an average of 
18.5 days in India, among the longest stays globally. Greater 
international air connectivity, easier visa processes, destination 
development, digital visitor services and stronger global 
promotion can help India convert its diverse cultural, spiritual, 
natural and experiential offerings into a larger share of global 
tourism demand.
Key Industry Trends and Growth Drivers
Favourable demographics are expanding the travel market
India’s young and expanding working-age population, rising 
disposable incomes and urbanisation are creating a favourable 
environment for travel demand. The World Economic Forum 
estimates that middle-class and affluent consumers will 
account for 93% of India’s total consumer spending by 2036, 
up from 80% in 2026. Further, the World Economic Forum 
estimates that middle-class and affluent consumers could 
account for 93% of India’s total consumer spending by 2036, 
compared with 80% in 2026. Rising purchasing power and 
greater discretionary spending are expected to support higher 
spending on leisure, experiences and travel.
Infrastructure development is improving accessibility
India’s operational airport network has expanded from 74 
airports in 2014 to more than 160 in 2025, supported by new 
terminals, greenfield airports and modernisation of existing 
191
facilities. The Airports Authority of India plans to invest  
~`150 bn by 2028 in air traffic control automation, navigation 
systems and related infrastructure. The expansion of modern 
rail connectivity is also supporting tourism, with 39.8 mn 
passengers travelling on Vande Bharat trains in FY2025-26, up 
nearly 34% y-o-y.
Regional connectivity is opening new tourism markets
The expansion of secondary airports and regional aviation is 
improving access to smaller cities and emerging destinations. 
Under UDAN, 679 routes across 95 airports, heliports and 
water aerodromes had been operationalised by 2026, carrying 
more than 16.8 mn passengers. The Modified UDAN scheme, 
with an outlay of `288.4 bn, is expected to further strengthen 
connectivity across underserved regions.
International travel is becoming more accessible
Visa facilitation and expanding flight connectivity are lowering 
barriers to international travel. India’s e-Visa facility, which 
initially covered 43 countries in 2014, had expanded to 172 
countries by August 2025, with 3.17 mn tourist e-Visas issued 
between November 2024 and November 2025.
Airline capacity and network expansion are strengthening 
mobility
India’s aviation ecosystem is gaining capacity through 
new entrants and expanding networks. During FY 2025-26, 
three new airlines, Shankh Air, Al Hind Air and FlyExpress, 
received No-Objection Certificates from the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation. Existing airlines are also expanding domestic and 
international routes, including direct long-haul connectivity 
using next-generation aircraft. Together, these developments 
are improving travel options and supporting the growth of both 
domestic and international tourism.
Domestic, Leisure and Experiential Travel
The expansion of the middle class, rising travel propensity 
and improved connectivity are creating more travel occasions 
across the country. Short-haul holidays, staycations, destination 
weddings, curated experiences and regional travel are gaining 
traction, while digital platforms are making travel discovery, 
planning and booking more accessible and personalised.
Spiritual, Heritage and Cultural Tourism
Spiritual tourism remains a significant driver of domestic 
travel, with large-scale events such as Maha Kumbh 2025 and 
continued investments in pilgrimage destinations supporting 
visitor flows and local economic activity. This momentum is 
being reinforced through Swadesh Darshan 2.0, under which 
52 projects worth `21.09  bn have been sanctioned, covering 
destinations such as Bodh Gaya, Chitrakoot, Khatu Shyam 
Ji, Mamallapuram and Hampi. The focus is shifting towards 
experience-led destinations, including cultural, spiritual, 
heritage, wellness and rural experiences, which can encourage 
tourists to spend more time and explore beyond the primary 
attraction.The PRASHAD (Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage 
Augmentation Drive) scheme, with 48 projects across 27 
States and Union Territories, is complementing this through 
investments in pilgrim amenities, facilitation centres, parking, 
ghats, cleanliness, safety and accessibility. Such infrastructure 
can improve visitor capacity and experience while supporting 
employment, local skills and community livelihoods. The 
development of connected tourism experiences around 
pilgrimage and heritage sites can also expand opportunities for 
accommodation, transport, food, handicrafts and local retail, 
enabling tourism spending to reach a wider set of businesses 
and communities.
Wellness, Medical and Niche Tourism
India’s healthcare capabilities, cost competitiveness, Ayurveda 
and wellness ecosystem are strengthening its position in 
medical and wellness tourism. The country ranked among 
the leading global destinations for both medical and wellness 
tourism, while adventure, wildlife, eco-tourism, cruise, rural and 
MICE tourism are creating additional avenues for destination-
led growth. In 2025, 507,244 foreign nationals travelled to India 
for medical treatment, accounting for around 5.5% of FTAs.
Connectivity and Digitalisation
Air and surface connectivity continues to expand India’s 
tourism map, improving access to emerging destinations 
and supporting leisure and business travel. India’s airport 
infrastructure has expanded significantly, with annual 
passenger-handling capacity exceeding 580 million, compared 
with around 420 million passengers handled in FY 2025-26. 
The country now has 166 airports, with 14 of 25 approved 
greenfield airports already operationalised, while Indian airlines 
have 860 aircraft in operation and 2,056 aircraft on order, 
creating substantial capacity for future travel demand.
Passenger traffic growth, however, has moderated amid 
geopolitical tensions, aircraft availability constraints and 
operational disruptions. ICRA estimates overall airport 
passenger traffic to have reached 419-422 million in FY 2025-
26, with growth expected to rebound to 435-445 million in 
FY 2026-27 as domestic leisure and business travel and 
international connectivity strengthen. At the same time, 
digital platforms, online travel services and technology-led 
travel planning are making destination discovery, booking and 
trip management increasingly seamless, supporting a more 
connected and digitally enabled tourism ecosystem.
Policy and Infrastructure Support
Government policy continued to focus on making tourism a 
stronger engine of economic growth, employment and regional 
development. The Union Budget 2026-27 further shifted 
the emphasis towards destination competitiveness, skills, 
digitalisation and development of new tourism experiences.
Key measures include the proposed establishment of a National 
Institute of Hospitality, upskilling of 10,000 tourist guides across 
20 iconic destinations, creation of a National Destination Digital 
=== page 99 ===
192
Knowledge Grid, development of sustainable mountain, turtle 
and bird-watching trails, transformation of 15 archaeological 
sites into vibrant experiential destinations, development of 
Buddhist circuits in the North-East, and creation of five tourism 
destinations across the Purvodaya states.
Challenges
The underlying demand was accompanied by periods of 
significant disruption during FY 2025-26. The Pahalgam terror 
attack in April 2025 resulted in widespread cancellations and 
a sharp deterioration in travel sentiment towards Jammu 
& Kashmir during the peak travel season. The incident 
demonstrated the sensitivity of tourism demand to safety 
and security concerns and highlighted the importance of 
destination preparedness and traveller confidence.
Air travel also experienced periods of heightened uncertainty 
during the year, with safety-related developments affecting 
traveller sentiment and reinforcing the importance of confidence 
in aviation and travel infrastructure. Such events highlighted 
the interconnected nature of tourism, transportation and 
traveller confidence, particularly for destinations and journeys 
with a high dependence on air connectivity.
Natural disasters and extreme weather events presented 
another challenge, with floods, flash floods, cloudbursts and 
landslides disrupting connectivity and travel across several 
tourism-dependent regions. These disruptions reinforced 
the need for climate-resilient tourism infrastructure, stronger 
destination preparedness and diversification of tourism 
circuits.
Geopolitical developments also continued to influence 
international travel. The escalation of the West Asia conflict in 
early 2026 disrupted air connectivity and affected travel to and 
through the region, with implications for India’s inbound and 
outbound travel flows. While India’s predominantly domestic 
demand base provides some insulation, prolonged geopolitical 
uncertainty could affect international arrivals, business travel 
and traveller sentiment.
Outlook
The outlook for FY 2026-27 and beyond remains favourable, 
supported by rising travel propensity, strong domestic 
demand, infrastructure development and a widening range of 
tourism experiences. WTTC expects India’s Travel & Tourism 
contribution to increase 8.5% in CY 2026 to US$286.1 billion, 
with employment supported by the sector reaching 48.1 
million.
The next phase of growth will increasingly depend on broadening 
India’s tourism footprint and capturing greater international 
demand. Developing new destinations, strengthening 
connectivity, simplifying visitor access, enhancing digital travel 
services and positioning India’s spiritual, cultural, natural, 
wellness and experiential offerings can help expand both 
visitor volumes and spend.At the same time, security incidents, geopolitical tensions, 
extreme weather and infrastructure disruptions will remain 
important risks. The industry’s ability to diversify source 
markets and destinations, strengthen preparedness and 
respond rapidly to changing travel patterns will be critical to 
sustaining growth.
Overall, FY 2025-26 reinforced the scale and depth of India’s 
travel opportunity. With a strong domestic base and significant 
headroom in international tourism, the sector is entering 
its next phase with the opportunity to move from recovery-
led growth towards a broader, more diversified and globally 
competitive tourism ecosystem.
Indian Hospitality Industry Overview
The Indian hospitality industry maintained strong momentum 
during FY 2025-26, supported by resilient domestic leisure 
travel, MICE, weddings and business travel. Favourable 
demand-supply dynamics, with premium room additions 
continuing to lag demand in key markets, supported occupancy 
and pricing. ICRA estimates industry revenues grew by ~11% 
in FY 2025-26.
Premium hotel occupancy remained healthy at 72–74%, while 
Average Room Rates (ARRs) increased to `8,200–8,500, 
supporting strong operating leverage and profitability. ICRA 
estimates operating margins for its sample of large premium 
hotel companies at around 37%, well above pre-pandemic 
levels.
Demand remained largely supported by the domestic market, 
cushioning the impact of a 7.9% decline in foreign tourist 
arrivals in CY 2025 amid geopolitical disruptions and security 
concerns. New hotel supply is increasingly expanding into Tier 
II and Tier III cities, airport locations and spiritual destinations, 
while asset-light models continue to support footprint 
expansion.
Outlook
The industry is expected to maintain its growth trajectory in 
FY 2026-27, albeit at a more moderate pace. ICRA projects 
revenue growth of 7–9%, with premium hotel occupancy at 
72–74% and ARR rising to `8,600–8,800. Domestic leisure, 
MICE, weddings and business travel are expected to remain key 
demand drivers, while improving connectivity, infrastructure 
and India’s growing positioning as an events and investment 
destination could support inbound demand.
However, prolonged geopolitical tensions, particularly the 
West Asia conflict, inflationary pressures and weaker travel 
sentiment could moderate the pace of growth.
Business Overview
Founded in 1881, we are India’s leading integrated travel and 
travel-related financial services company, headquartered 
in Mumbai and backed by the Fairfax Group, which holds a 
63.83% equity stake. We operate across 28 countries and five 
continents through more than 800 customer touchpoints, with 
193
a diversified portfolio spanning Travel and Related Services, 
Financial Services, Leisure Hospitality & Resorts and Digital 
Imaging Solutions. Our businesses are built around 16 brands 
and supported by a workforce of more than 10,000 employees, 
with over 145 years of operating experience.
During the year, we continued to strengthen our businesses 
through focused expansion, digital innovation and strategic 
initiatives. Travel and Related Services remained our largest 
contributor to consolidated revenue, while Financial Services, 
Leisure Hospitality & Resorts and Digital Imaging Solutions 
continued to expand their market presence and customer 
reach.
Our long-term credit rating was upgraded to ‘CRISIL AA/
Stable’, reflecting our strong financial profile. We also 
continued to maintain a strong financial profile and disciplined 
capital management. CRISIL reaffirmed our ‘CRISIL AA/Stable’ 
long-term and corporate credit ratings and ‘CRISIL A1+’ short-
term rating in April 2026, retaining the highest rating awarded 
to a travel and tourism company in India. The reaffirmation 
reflected our leadership across Travel and Foreign Exchange,

strong liquidity. CRISIL also recognised the continued support 
of Fairfax Financial Holdings, alongside our disciplined cost 
management and the proposed demerger of the resorts and

Value-Added Services (VAS)
During FY 2025-26, we repositioned our Value-Added Services 
(VAS) vertical from an ancillary portfolio into a core part of our 
customer proposition. Our offerings span travel insurance, 
travel assurance, visa protection, medical and pre-existing 
illness cover, emergency assistance, and visa and passport 
facilitation across Leisure, MICE, Corporate Travel and 
Financial Services.
We introduced two industry-first propositions during the year. 
TravSure, launched across Thomas Cook India and SOTC 
Travel, provides complimentary rescheduling and refunds for 
eligible emergencies, additional trip protection of up to USD 
1,500 per traveller, 24x7 support and emergency coverage for 
war, political unrest, riots, flight suspensions, trip curtailments 
and airspace closures. Visa Rejection Cover, underwritten by 
ICICI Lombard, protects non-recoverable advance payments 
towards travel and accommodation in the event of visa denial 
and is available across group tours, FIT holidays, MICE and 
Corporate Travel.
We expanded the portfolio with Pre-Existing Illness Cover for 
travellers aged 60 years and above, a senior travel ecosystem 
with GenSLife, Marzi and Ananta, and terrain-specific insurance 
for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. Our prepaid cards also carry 
complimentary insurance, emergency cash assistance and 
chip-and-PIN fraud protection, with the Study Buddy Card 
offering cover suited to students overseas. Travel insurance 
is integrated into our managed Corporate Travel and MICE 
programmes, while our integration with Atlys strengthened 
visa and passport facilitation by embedding foreign exchange 
within the visa application journey.
Digital integration across booking, servicing and claims 
platforms, supported by AI-enabled engagement and 24x7 
assistance, improved post-booking service. The VAS portfolio 
also provides higher-margin, asset-light revenue opportunities 
while strengthening customer confidence and repeat 
engagement.
Our Travel Business Associate (TBA) programme expanded

supplementary income for homemakers, micro-entrepreneurs 
and small business owners, while TBA Plus partners 
independently manage bookings through dedicated codes and

accounting for 22% of passengers booked online for leisure

170 PSA and GSA touchpoints and 17 airport counters. More 
than 200 active Travel Business Associates contributed ~9% 
of overall business volumes, with digitally enabled TBA Plus 
partners managing bookings through dedicated codes and 
self-service capabilities.

SOTC Travel Limited
SOTC Travel Limited continued to strengthen its position in 
the organised leisure travel market through its omnichannel 
‘phygital’ model, diversified portfolio and customer-centric 
offerings.
Spiritual tourism remained an important growth area through 
the Darshans portfolio. The portfolio was enhanced through 
curated itineraries, aerial darshans, VIP temple access and 
specialised services.
Customer convenience remained a key focus, with the 
introduction of TravSure, offering free rescheduling, emergency 
cancellation, additional trip protection and 24/7 assistance, 
alongside an industry-first Visa Rejection Cover. SOTC also

assisted sales.

through destination diversification, spiritual tourism,

financing and technology-enabled engagement.
TC Tours Limited
TC Tours Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Thomas 
Cook (India) Limited, offers a comprehensive range of travel 
services, including air ticketing, hotel bookings, domestic tours 
and related travel solutions. During the year, the Company 
expanded its offerings across leisure travel, corporate travel 
and MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions), 
catering to the diverse requirements of its customer segments. 
Integrated within the broader Group ecosystem, TC Tours 
leveraged its capabilities and network to deliver seamless, 
end-to-end travel solutions across customer needs.
Travel Circle International Limited – Hong Kong
During FY 2025-26, Travel Circle International Limited, Hong 
Kong’s leading tour operator in the upscale all-inclusive 
long-haul leisure segment, navigated a challenging operating 
environment marked by heightened geopolitical tensions, 
renewed U.S. tariff measures, cautious consumer spending 
and rising travel costs. The company’s business remained 
predominantly B2C, contributing ~95% of sales through three 
retail stores, a call centre and its website, while the balance 
was generated through third-party B2B channels.
Intensifying competition from mass-market operators and 
players replicating premium itineraries at lower price points 
increased pricing pressure and affected customer retention, 
while higher airfares and land costs weighed on margins.Key initiatives:
• Against this backdrop, the company focused on 
strengthening differentiation, advancing its summer 
and winter programmes to secure early bookings, and 
enhancing customer value through distinctive, high-
quality travel experiences.
• The company broadened and optimised its product 
portfolio with differentiated experiences across key 
destinations and travel formats. New and enhanced 
offerings included Isère and Rhône and Seine River cruises 
in Europe; Dolomites and luxury truffle festival experiences 
in Italy; Antarctica, South Georgia and Falkland Islands 
journeys in South America; Western Africa cruise 
itineraries; and premium China programmes combining 
luxury seasonal trains and cruises around floral and 
autumn foliage seasons, including the Silk Road Express. 
In Asia, the portfolio was strengthened through the Eastern 
& Oriental Express with Thailand and premium Mekong 
River cruise itineraries covering Vietnam, Cambodia and 
Laos.
• China also emerged as a key growth market, with the 
company focusing on premium and in-depth journeys 
beyond highly competitive cross-border routes and 
exploring less-saturated destinations. The launch of a new 
themed tour series, supported by targeted promotions, 
complemented this strategy.
• To strengthen market awareness and customer 
engagement, the company conducted product showcases 
and carnival-style events in Hong Kong and Macau, 
alongside its participation in major travel exhibitions and 
collaborations with airlines, tourism boards and credit 
card partners.
• Customer experience remained a key operational priority, 
supported by a three-tier customer contact mechanism 
covering the pre-travel, during-travel and post-travel 
stages. Customer scores across service and destination 
experience improved to 9.0/10 from 8.8/10 in 2025, while 
service scores increased to 9.7/10 from 9.6/10. Post-tour 
reviews conducted for each tour series and destination 
enabled the company to establish service benchmarks 
and continuously refine its offerings.
• Marketing efforts combined personalised direct marketing, 
remarketing and member engagement with digital 
advertising, high-quality content, print media, television 
commercials, flagship product launches and offline events. 
These initiatives expanded audience reach, increased 
digital engagement and supported customer retention and 
early bookings.
 Looking ahead, the company will continue to strengthen 
its premium positioning through differentiated products, 
immersive digital and virtual tour content, deeper 
strategic partnerships and expansion into new markets,

Corporate Travel
Our Corporate Travel business reported net revenue of `1,541 
mn during FY 2025-26, up 19% year-on-year, supported 
by increasing demand for integrated travel management 
solutions and strong growth in non-air services. We served 
more than 800 corporate clients through end-to-end solutions 
spanning air, hotel, rail, car rentals, corporate cards and travel 
insurance.
Non-air services continued to grow faster than core air 
ticketing, with hotel volumes increasing 7.6% and hotel 
transaction density rising 10.7%, reflecting deeper engagement 
across existing accounts. Gross Transaction Value stood at 
`27 bn, while air volumes grew 4.8%, including 7.4% growth 
in international air volumes. The air-to-non-air revenue mix 
stood at 84:16. Touchless transactions accounted for ~53% of 
total transactions, while online booking tool adoption reached 
32% of clients.
Our client base remained diversified across industries, with 
information technology, manufacturing and industrial, banking 
and financial services, healthcare and pharmaceuticals and 
other sectors.
Corporate Travel remains structurally resilient, with demand 
driven largely by business requirements rather than 
discretionary spending. India is now the ninth-largest business 
travel market globally and the fourth-largest in Asia-Pacific. 
During the year, we also partnered with Booking.com to expand 
accommodation options for corporate clients.
We strengthened our digital capabilities through our self-
booking platform to simplify and automate booking workflows. 
We also established Travel Circle International (Cyprus) Limited 
in Nicosia, our first European Union office, and commenced 
direct air and hotel booking operations from this base. The 
entity strengthens our ability to serve Indian corporates and 
multinational clients across the EU, negotiate local supplier 
pricing and access regional inventory. For further details, 
please refer to the Integrated Report on page 64.
MICE
Our MICE business reported revenue of `13,364 mn during FY 
2025-26, supported by sustained demand from corporates, 
government projects and large-format events. We managed 
more than 420 corporate groups across domestic and 
international destinations and served over 100,000 travellers, 
an increase of 19%. The revenue mix comprised 85% 
international and 15% domestic.Key client sectors included BFSI, FMCG, industrial and 
manufacturing, healthcare and pharmaceuticals. We 
supported programmes ranging from four to more than 3,000 
delegates through a network of over 500 tour managers, 
destination reconnaissance, venue validation and established 
local partner ecosystems.
We further strengthened our capabilities in complex international 
assignments through programmes including International Solar 
Alliance regional meetings in Sri Lanka, Chile and Ghana, the 
Eighth Assembly in New Delhi involving delegates from more 
than 150 countries, and the Asian Aquatic Championships 
2025, where we served as the exclusive travel, transport and 
accommodation partner for more than 1,100 athletes, officials 
and dignitaries.
Our digital initiatives supported execution through the Customer 
Service System (CSS App) for delegate registration, visa 
documentation and payment collection, and Tour Pe, used by 
more than 500 tour managers for real-time itinerary, expense, 
trip wallet, passenger detail and feedback management. For 
further details, please refer to the Integrated Report on page 60.
India Destination Management Services
Our India Destination Management Services (DMS) business 
reported revenue from operations of `6,467 mn during FY 
2025-26, up 3% year-on-year. Demand remained diversified 
across international source markets, led by the United 
Kingdom, France, Germany and the United States.
Operating through Travel Corporation (India) Limited and its 
brands Sita, TCI, Distant Frontiers and Vilasita, complemented 
by GoVacation India, TropiCulture and Aranya by SITA, we 
expanded our offerings across wildlife, sports, luxury and 
experiential tourism. Our network comprises 30 offices across 
India and South Asia, 21 overseas sales representatives and 
more than 2,500 agents and partners, serving inbound leisure, 
luxury, MICE, wildlife and customised FIT travellers across 
India, Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka.
We advanced our digital transformation through Travart, our 
comprehensive travel technology platform integrating product 
management, costing, pricing and finance.
We also continued to strengthen sustainable and responsible 
tourism practices, with SITA achieving Travelife Certified status 
at ITB Berlin 2025, reflecting compliance with more than 200 
internationally recognised sustainability criteria aligned with 
ISO 26000 and the UN-supported Global Sustainable Tourism 
Criteria. For further details, please refer to the Integrated Report 
on page 69.

Our International DMS business reported revenue of `29,092 
mn, up 3% year-on-year, across 28 countries and 5 continents. 
Performance was supported by growth in Asian Trails by 18%, 
Private Safaris Southern Africa by 34%, Private Safaris East 
Africa by 18% and AlliedTPro by 9%. Whereas, the Middle East 
operations moderated in line with regional travel conditions

Leisure Hospitality & Resorts
Our Leisure Hospitality & Resorts business continued 
to strengthen its position in India’s growing experiential 
hospitality market during FY 2025-26, supported by demand 
across leisure, spiritual, MICE, destination weddings and 
bleisure segments. Sterling Holiday Resorts Limited remained 
the foundation of our portfolio, operating 78 resorts across 65 
destinations with 3,810 operational rooms.
We closed the year with our 25th consecutive profitable 
quarter, while remaining debt-free with cash reserves of `3,395 
mn. Consolidated occupancy was maintained at 59%, despite a 
17% expansion in room inventory, while ARR remained broadly 
stable at `6,176 versus `6,263 in the previous year. Total 
segment revenue grew 6.6% to `5,336 mn, EBITDA increased 
3% to `1,753 mn at a 33% margin, and segment EBIT stood at 
`1,292 mn at a 24% margin. Resort operations revenue grew 
19% to `4,207 mn, supported by 20% growth in room revenues 
and 13% growth in food and beverage revenues.
EBIT growth was supported by resort-led income, which now 
represents ~85%–90% of the operating model. The guest ratio 
remained at 75%, while the second half outperformed the first 
by more than 21%.
Sterling continued to expand through an asset-right model, 
with 62% of our portfolio comprising owned, leased and 
revenue-share properties and 38% managed properties. 17 
resorts were added during the year.
Nature Trails, our adventure-retreat brand within the Leisure 
Hospitality & Resorts portfolio and focusses on immersive 
stays in scenic natural settings across hills, forests and 
waterfront locations. It caters to diverse segments including 
FIT holidays, weddings, MICE events, reunions, picnics and 
educational trips.
During FY 2025-26, the brand catered to key customer 
segments and the demand for experiential and nature-led 
hospitality. Expansion momentum continued with five new 
management signings across Dodamarg, Rishikesh, Hampi 
and Goa.As part of the Group’s strategic restructuring, the six Nature 
Trails resorts are being consolidated with Sterling Holiday 
Resorts Limited enabling a more focused and scalable leisure 
hospitality platform.
Key Developments
• We expanded across leisure, spiritual and business 
destinations including Ayodhya, Gangtok, Dharamshala, 
Mohali, Sakleshpur, Vellore and Hampi, alongside Sterling 
Amargarh Jodhpur, Sterling Nirmaya Dharamshala, 
Sterling Valley of Pine Lansdowne, Sterling Saryu Ayodhya, 
Sterling Avante Mohali and Nature Trails Ashoka Resorts

combining owned assets, management contracts and

resorts rated 4.5 or above, and 25 resorts ranked first in

Booking.com Traveller Review Awards, with Sterling 
Kanha and Doon Diner at Sterling Mussoorie ranking in the 
worldwide top 1% of their categories.
• Our proprietary Sterling ONE B2B distribution platform, 
powered by distributed ledger technology, connects more 
than 7,000 travel partners and 360 corporate clients to 
resort inventory and food and beverage offerings. We also 
deployed an integrated hospitality property management 
system and AI-enabled guest journey tools.

Kodai Valley added 32 suites, while Sterling Munnar

Refurbishment and infrastructure upgrades were 
undertaken at Sterling Kodai Lake, Nainital and Yercaud, 
while the Katha restaurant at Jaisinghgarh, Udaipur

renewable energy, energy efficiency and responsible 
resource management. The Heat Pump Programme was 
completed across seven resorts, delivering estimated 
annual energy savings of ~350,000 kWh, alongside fast-
charging EV stations across resorts and three hospitality 
training centres established with state governments. For 
further details, please refer to the Integrated Report on

Proposed Demerger
As part of our strategic restructuring, TCIL proposed the 
demerger of its Resort business into Sterling Holiday Resorts 
Limited (SHRL) under a Composite Scheme of Arrangement to 
enable greater strategic and operational focus.
As a part of the scheme, SHRL, a company with significant 
expertise in the hospitality sector, is expected to enable 
focused growth and operational efficiencies while facilitating 
the creation of a dedicated hospitality platform. SHRL will be 
listed on the main board of BSE and NSE, upon completion of 
all regulatory formalities. For further details, please refer to the 
Board’s Report on page 133 .  
Digital Imaging Solutions
Our Digital Imaging Solutions business, operated through 
our 51% stake in DEI Holdings Limited (DEI), continued to 
strengthen its position as a global leader in souvenir imaging 
services. Headquartered in Dubai, DEI operates across 14 
countries, 264 sites and 8 regional offices, serving theme 
parks, aquariums, water parks, cable cars, luxury hotels and 
other leading attractions.
DEI operates a partnership-led model with 125 long-term 
partnerships, recording 108 mn imaging captures during 
the year. The UAE remained its largest contributor at ~50% 
of revenue, with additional operations across Singapore, 
Malaysia, Indonesia, Egypt, India, Thailand, Greater China, 
Saudi Arabia, Oman and the Maldives.
During the year, the company focused on operational 
optimisation, technology-led transformation and selective 
portfolio expansion. Performance benefited from productivity 
improvements, cost discipline and operating efficiencies 
across key markets. However, moderation in Middle East 
visitor footfalls on account of geopolitical conflict in the 
region, particularly in the latter part of the year, affected the 
UAE business. The company responded by aligning workforce 
deployment with demand, increasing the use of proprietary 
platforms and AI-led automation, and renegotiating selected 
site rentals. Growth in Hong Kong and Malaysia provided 
support, while 15 new partner sites were contracted across 
Indonesia, Singapore, China, Macau SAR and Hong Kong. For 
further details, please refer to the Integrated Report on page 82 .

Shared Services
The captive Shared Services Centre (SSC) continues to provide 
business support to serve as a key pillar in the delivery of the 
Group’s business and financial objectives.
Its principal mandate is to drive operational efficiency and 
enable the realization of synergies across the Group’s 
constituent entities.
In pursuit, the SSC maintains a sustained focus on process 
optimization, supported by the deployment of advanced 
digital technologies, cloud-based infrastructure and bespoke 
reporting frameworks. These initiatives are directed towards 
enhancing operational efficiency and strengthening the quality 
and timeliness of management information available to the 
Group.
Given the prevailing business environment, the SSC has 
placed heightened emphasis on improving service delivery and 
customer experience across the Group. This reflects the SSC’s 
continued commitment to anticipating and responding to 
the Group’s evolving operational priorities, while concurrently 
managing an increasingly complex and demanding regulatory 
and compliance environment.
Through the consistent execution of these initiatives, the SSC 
remains closely aligned with the Group’s overarching strategic 
priorities, while preserving the flexibility and responsiveness 
required to operate effectively within a continually evolving 
business landscape.

Cash Conservation
The Company remains committed to meeting the evolving

Credit Ratings Upgraded by CRISIL
On 31st March 2026, CRISIL Ratings has reaffirmed the long-
term rating and corporate credit rating (CCR) of Thomas Cook 
(India) Limited (TCIL) at ‘CRISIL AA/Stable’, along with its short-
term rating at ‘CRISIL A1+’. The reaffirmation underscores the 
Group’s resilient business model, strong financial profile and 
consistent operational performance, even amidst a dynamic 
and evolving global environment.Yield Optimisation in a falling interest rate regime
The falling interest rates continued for major part of FY 2025-
26 and evidenced interest rate stabilization between end of 
2025 & mid 2026. This continued to pose challenges on yield 
on investments for corporates. Following the ‘Safety First’ 
principle, as always, the Company prioritised investments in 
bank deposits, select corporate deposits/ bonds and selectively 
invested in a limited number of mutual funds, all of which were 
in line with the pre-approved board policy. In response to the 
global decline in interest rates for multiple currencies, we 
continued to adopt strategies to enhance yield. This involved 
extensive usage of currency swaps to move funds across 
currencies and countries on a fully hedged basis while also 
diversifying into investment alternatives within the ambit of 
aforementioned board approvals.
Support to Subsidiaries
As business activity normalised across most geographies 
during FY 2025-26, the need for inter-company financial 
assistance to Indian and overseas subsidiaries significantly 
declined, with support extended sparingly. Selective aid was 
provided to subsidiaries affected by geopolitical tensions 
in the Middle East. The Company continued to encourage 
subsidiaries to become independent by increasing bank lines 
wherever needed by working closely with the central treasury 
team.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
We continued to strengthen our commitment to inclusive 
growth and community impact through focused healthcare 
and sustainability initiatives during FY 2025-26. As a Trustee 
of the Fairfax India Charitable Foundation (FICF), we continue 
to support the nationwide dialysis initiative aimed at improving 
access to affordable and quality dialysis treatment across 
underserved regions in India.Chronic kidney disease remains a significant healthcare 
challenge in India, particularly given limited access to 
affordable dialysis treatment across rural and semi-urban 
regions. In partnership with hospitals and state authorities, our 
company supported the deployment of dialysis infrastructure 
under a public-private partnership model. The initiative aims 
to expand access to free or subsidised dialysis treatment, 
reduce the financial burden on patients and improve long-term 
healthcare outcomes.
By the close of FY 2025-26, our programme had reached 30 
States and Union Territories and 305 districts, supporting 419 
dialysis centres with 1,601 dialysis machines operational. 
Cumulatively, 3.73 mn free or low-cost dialysis sessions 
have been delivered, creating estimated savings of `7.4 bn 
for patients and generating 4,180 jobs. The programme is 
supported by 25 implementation partners, contributes nearly 
10% of all dialysis machines deployed under the Pradhan 
Mantri National Dialysis Programme, and has improved 
access to quality dialysis closer to home for an estimated 38% 
of the rural population.
During the year, our company in partnership with FICF also 
expanded our social impact beyond healthcare through our 
first vocational education initiative, supporting underprivileged 
children at Dhondegaon School, Nashik. Our contribution of 
`1.7 mn funded an additional Skill Development workshop 
facility to provide hands-on training in cycle repairing, 
fabrication and hydroponics. The initiative benefits more than 
450 students, training them across over 10 vocational skill 
sets, supporting employability, entrepreneurship and efforts to 
reduce school dropout rates among tribal youth.
We also continue our decade-long support to the Swachh 
Bharat Abhiyan through the maintenance of prefabricated, 
eco-friendly public toilets in Ooty. For further details, please 
refer to the Integrated Report on page 104.

Risk Management
Balancing Opportunity and Risk
At Thomas Cook, we place strong emphasis on a robust risk management framework to effectively navigate the complexities of our 
multinational operations. Our integrated approach encompasses ongoing risk identification, assessment, mitigation, monitoring, 
and reporting. By aligning risk management with our strategic goals, we adopt a holistic stance that not only addresses potential 
threats but also capitalises on emerging opportunities. This proactive and structured approach enables us to drive sustainable 
growth, build organisational resilience, and uphold the long-term trust of our stakeholders.
Identifying and mitigating risks remains fundamental to ensuring the Company’s resilience and long-term success. Thomas Cook 
(India) Limited has instituted a robust risk management framework that is regularly reviewed by senior management. The key risks 
identified, along with well-defined mitigation strategies, are outlined below:
Risk Description Mitigation Measures
Cybersecurity & 
Information SecurityIncreased reliance on 
technology exposes the 
organization to cybersecurity 
threats, potential service 
disruption, and data breaches• Risk-based, layered cybersecurity framework supported by robust 
policies, standards, and procedures.
• Continuous threat monitoring, threat intelligence, and incident 
response capabilities to detect and respond to cyber threats and 
minimize business disruption.
• Regular security assessments, vulnerability management, and control 
enhancements to proactively address emerging risks.
• Strong employee security awareness and engagement to strengthen 
the organization’s human layer of defence.
• Cyber resilience and recovery capabilities to ensure critical services 
and business operations can be restored quickly following a cyber 
incident.
Data Privacy Risk Non-compliance with 
contractual and regulatory 
data privacy requirements can 
lead to fines, litigation, and 
reputational damage• Privacy policies and standards are being strengthened to align with 
applicable regulatory and contractual data privacy requirements.
• Privacy and security controls are being enhanced to strengthen the 
protection of Personal Data throughout its lifecycle.
• DPDP governance, processes, and accountability mechanisms are 
being established as part of the organization's ongoing DPDP Act, 
2023 readiness programme.
• Regular employee awareness and third-party privacy assessments 
are being strengthened to support sustainable privacy compliance.
Geopolitical Risk Global geopolitical instability 
can impact safety, mobility, 
and business continuity.• Continuous global monitoring to proactively manage potential 
disruptions.
• Implementation of insurance coverages and contingency plans to 
protect customers, employees and operations.
Foreign Exchange 
(Forex) RiskExposure to currency 
fluctuations due to global 
operations may affect financial 
performance.• Robust hedging policy in place.
• Active monitoring of currency markets and proactive forex 
Management through hedging contracts.
Regulatory &

reputational damage.• A centralised compliance management system is in place to monitor 
and track all regulatory, statutory, and licensing requirements across 
jurisdictions, ensuring adherence as well as timely renewals.
• Periodic governance reviews and stringent monitoring protocols are 
actively conducted to ensure continuous compliance with applicable 
laws, regulations, and contractual obligations.
Credit Risk Delayed or inadequate 
recoveries from customers 
and counterparties may 
adversely impact liquidity and

• Financial evaluations of major clients and partners by the finance

• Strategic adaptability to ensure resilience in operations and travel

203
Internal Control Systems and Their Adequacy
At Thomas Cook India, robust internal control systems are 
embedded across all functions and processes. These systems 
are continuously reviewed and strengthened to enhance 
operational efficiency, effectiveness, risk management, and 
governance. An annual Internal Audit plan, approved by the 
Audit Committee, ensures systematic evaluation of business 
processes and controls. This is complemented by IT Auditors, 
Internal Financial Control Auditors, and Statutory Auditors, 
who independently assess the adequacy and effectiveness of 
internal controls, including controls over financial reporting.
In compliance with RBI guidelines, the Company has instituted 
Concurrent Auditing for its Foreign Exchange operations across 
branches. The Anti-Money Laundering (AML) framework is 
regularly updated to reflect evolving regulatory requirements. 
The Company also maintains appropriate controls and 
monitoring mechanisms to safeguard information assets, 
support data privacy obligations, and ensure adherence to 
audit trail requirements.Audit findings and recommendations are discussed with 
Senior Management, and corrective actions are periodically 
monitored. The Audit Committee reviews key audit 
observations and the status of remediation on a quarterly 
basis, reinforcing a culture of accountability, compliance, and 
continuous improvement.
Forward-looking Statements
This Management Discussion and Analysis Report contains 
certain forward-looking statements reflecting the Company’s 
expectations regarding future business performance and 
industry developments. Actual results may differ materially 
due to factors including economic conditions, geopolitical 
developments, regulatory changes, foreign exchange 
fluctuations, inflationary pressures, travel demand trends, 
climate-related disruptions, technological developments, and 
other external factors impacting the travel, tourism, hospitality, 
and foreign exchange industries.

Report of the Directors on Corporate Governance
1. COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON THE CODE OF CORPORATE GOVERNANCE:
 Thomas Cook (India) Limited (“TCIL/Company”) philosophy on Corporate Governance is to conduct its business in a manner 
which is ethical and transparent with all stakeholders of the Company. The Company believes in providing a structure that works 
for the benefit of everyone concerned, by ensuring that the Company adheres to ethical standards, laws and best practices.  
The Company’s policy on Corporate Governance is to make it a way of life by, inter-alia , adopting standard Corporate Governance 
practices through continual improvement of internal systems and satisfaction of customers and shareholders. The Company 
in its approach to adopt the best possible practices of Corporate Governance and keeping adherence to the latest rules and 
regulations prescribed by various regulatory authorities, has taken all the necessary steps to stay in line with the continuously 
progressing governance demands.
 TCIL endeavours to demonstrate the highest standards of Corporate Governance and ethical behavior across all levels within 
the organisation with a zero-tolerance policy towards any deviation from these standards. Our ethical framework focuses on 
long term shareholder value creation through responsible decision making. As a global organisation, the Corporate Governance 
practices followed by the Company and its subsidiaries are compatible with international standards and practices.
 Our Corporate Governance framework ensures that we make timely disclosures and share relevant information regarding our 
financial performance, as well as disclosure related to the leadership and governance of the Company. At TCIL, Corporate 
Governance is more than just adherence to the statutory and regulatory requirements. It is equally about focusing on voluntary 
practices that underline the highest levels of transparency and propriety.
 Over the years, the Board of Directors has developed Corporate Governance guidelines to help fulfill our corporate responsibility 
towards the Company’s stakeholders. These guidelines ensure that the Board will have the necessary authority and processes 
to review and evaluate the Company’s operations when required. Further, these guidelines allow the Board to make decisions 
that are independent of the Management. The Board may change these guidelines as and when required, to achieve the 
Company’s stated objectives.
2. BOARD OF DIRECTORS (“BOARD”):
 TCIL, as a Company believes that an active, well informed and independent Board is necessary to ensure the highest standards 
of Corporate Governance. The Company believes that the Board is at the core of Corporate Governance and thus has optimum 
mix of Executive and Non-Executive Directors; including Woman Independent Director, which plays a significant role in ensuring 
the highest standards of Corporate Governance practice in the Company.
 Size and Composition of the Board:
 The Composition of the TCIL Board as on March 31, 2026, included Eight (8) members with one (1) Executive Director and 
Seven (7) Non-Executive Directors, of which four (4) were Independent Directors including one (1) Woman Independent Director, 
comprising of experts from various fields/professions.
 The composition of the Board of Directors of the Company is in accordance with the Securities and Exchange Board of India 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and the Companies Act, 2013, read with applicable rules 
made thereunder, as amended from time to time.
 Key Skills, Expertise and Competencies of the Board:
 The Board of Directors of TCIL comprises of qualified members who have the skills, expertise and competence to make 
effective contribution to the growth of the Company as well as on the various business and governance matters discussed in 
the Board and Committee meetings. The Board Members are committed to ensure that the Company is in compliance with the 
requisite standards of Corporate Governance.

Board Meetings:
The Meetings of the Board of Directors are scheduled well in advance and generally held at the Company’s Registered Office in 
Mumbai and all the necessary information and documents as required under Regulation 17(7) read with Part A of Schedule II of 
the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 pertaining to 
the meetings are made available to the Board of Directors. Senior Executives/ Management of the Company are invited to attend 
Meetings of the Board and Committees, to make presentations and provide clarifications as and when required. The Board meets 
at least once in a quarter to review the quarterly performance and approve the financial results.
With a view to leverage technology and reduce paper consumption since the year 2017, the Company has initiated convening of the 
Board and its Committee Meetings through electronic means which includes disseminating of documents such as Notices, Agendas, 
Notes etc. to the Directors through electronic means. Further, the minutes of the meetings are also circulated to the Directors via 
electronic mode. All the Directors have an access to the documents of the meeting on real time basis. Each Director has been 
provided with an iPad for the said purpose. This electronic mode of delivery of agenda papers, minutes and other documents not 
only ensures high standards of security and confidentiality, required for storage and circulation of Board papers but also increases 
the active involvement of the Board Members.
The Board met seven (7) times during the financial year ended March 31, 2026. The said meetings were held on May 12, 2025,  
May 30, 2025, July 30, 2025, November 12, 2025, December 18, 2025, February 5, 2026 and March 20, 2026, respectively.

Details of Directors to be appointed or re-appointed at ensuing Annual General Meeting:
(i) Re-appointment of Directors liable to retire by rotation at the 49th Annual General Meeting of the Company:
 Pursuant to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Articles of Association of the Company, two third of the Directors 
are liable to retire by rotation except Independent Directors who are not liable to retire by rotation. One third of these Directors 
shall retire every year by rotation and if eligible, shall qualify for re-appointment.
 In accordance with the provisions of Section 152 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Rules made there under and Article 
116 of the Articles of Association of the Company, Mr. Chandran Ratnaswami (DIN: 00109215) and Mr. Sumit Maheshwari 
(DIN: 06920646) are liable to retire by rotation at the ensuing Forty Ninth Annual General Meeting of the Company. However, 
Mr. Chandran Ratnaswami expressed his desire not to seek re-appointment due to his other pressing commitments within 
the Fairfax Group, consequently he will not be offering himself for re-appointment at the forthcoming Annual General Meeting. 
The Board, while noting his decision, places on record its sincere appreciation for the guidance, commitment, and valuable 
contributions rendered by Mr. Ratnaswami during his tenure of service. The Board also decided not to fill the vacancy caused 
by the retirement of Mr. Chandran Ratnaswami as the present composition of the Board of Directors is adequate and meets 
the compliance requirement. In terms of Section 152 of the Act, 2013, that, if the vacancy of the retiring director was not filled 
up, it would be required to be resolved expressly by the shareholders not to fill the vacancy of the retiring director. The said 
proposal for non-filling of the casual vacancy forms part of the Notice of the Forty Ninth Annual General Meeting and the 
relevant Resolution is recommended for the members approval therein.

3. COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD:
 To enable better and more focused attention on the affairs of the Company, the Board delegates particular matters to

(i) Audit Committee:
 The Board of Directors of the Company w.e.f. April 1, 2019 had changed the nomenclature and the charter of the Audit 
Committee to Audit cum Risk Management Committee.
 Further, pursuant to Regulation 18 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 read with Section 177 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 21 of the Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the Board vide its 
resolution dated September 10, 2021 had approved for constitution of Risk Management Committee and change 
in nomenclature of Audit cum Risk Management Committee to Audit Committee and also adopted the revised Audit 
Committee Charter which is further revised from time to time.
 The Audit Committee’s role flows directly from the Board’s overview function on Corporate Governance, which holds the 
management accountable to the Board and the Board accountable to the stakeholders.
 The Committee was originally formulated in August 1995 as Audit Committee and over the years the Committee has been 
reconstituted and its Charter has been amended from time to time to align it with the requirements of the applicable laws, 
rules and regulations.
 The present composition of the Audit Committee is in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and the 
rules made thereunder and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015. It consists of Six (6) Non-Executive Directors of whom four (4) are Independent as on March 31, 2026. 
The Chairperson of the Audit Committee is an Independent Director.
 The Audit Committee also invites at its meetings, senior executives/ management including the person in charge of the 
Business Process Improvement & Audit function of the Company. The Company Secretary & Compliance Officer acts 
as the Secretary to the Committee. The President & Group Chief Financial Officer and Chief Financial Officer are the 
special invitees to the Committee meetings. Further, the Chairperson, Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer, and the 
representatives of the Statutory Auditors are the permanent invitees to the Committee meetings.
 Terms of reference and role of the Audit Committee
 The terms of reference of the Audit Committee were amended from time to time to align the role of the Committee as 
per the amendments to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015. The terms of reference of the Committee are in accordance with the provisions of Section 177 of the 
Companies Act, 2013 read with the applicable rules made thereunder and Regulation 18 of the Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and as approved by the Board                    
inter-alia includes the following:
1. Oversight of the Company’s financial reporting process and the disclosure of its financial information to ensure that 
the financial statements are correct, sufficient and credible;
2. Recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of auditors of the Company;
3. Approval of payment to Statutory Auditors for any other services rendered by the Statutory Auditors;
4. Reviewing with the management, the quarterly and the Annual Financial Statements and Limited Review Report/ 
Auditor’s Report thereon before submission to the Board for approval, with particular reference to:
a. Matters required to be included in the Director’s Responsibility Statement to be included in the Board’s Report in 
terms of clause (c) of sub-section (3) of Section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013;
b. Changes, if any, in accounting policies and practices and reasons for the same;
c. Major accounting entries involving estimates based on the exercise of judgment by the management;
d. Significant adjustments made in the financial statements arising out of audit findings;
e. Disclosure/Approval of any related party transactions;
=== page 110 ===
214
f. Modified opinions and Qualifications, if any in the Draft Audit Report/ Limited Review Report;
g. Disclosure under Management Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations;
h. Compliance with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 and other legal requirements concerning financial statements;
i. Disclosure of contingent liabilities;
5. Reviewing with the management, the statement of uses / application of funds raised through an issue (public issue, 
rights issue, preferential issue etc.), the statement of funds utilized for purpose other than those stated in the offer 
documents / prospectus / notice and the report submitted by the monitoring agency for monitoring the utilization 
of proceeds of a public issue or rights issue or preferential issue or qualified institutions placement and making

approval;
7. Review and monitor the auditor’s independence and performance, and effectiveness of audit process;

9. Scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments;
10. Valuation of undertakings or assets of the Company, wherever it is necessary;
11. Evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems;
12. Reviewing, with the management, performance of statutory and internal auditors, adequacy of the internal control 
systems;
13. Reviewing the adequacy of internal audit function, if any, including the internal audit charter, the structure of the 
internal audit department, staffing and seniority of the official heading the department, reporting structure coverage

internal investigations by the Internal Auditors into matters where there is suspected fraud or irregularity or a failure of 
internal control systems of a material nature and reporting the matter to the board;
15. Discussion with Statutory Auditors before the audit commences, about the nature and scope of audit as well as  
post-audit discussion to ascertain any area of concern;
16. To look into the reasons for substantial defaults if any in the payment to the depositors, debenture holders, shareholders 
(in case of non-payment of declared dividends) and creditors;
17. To review the functioning of the Whistle Blower mechanism;
18. Approval of appointment of Chief Financial Officer after assessing the qualifications, experience and background, etc. 
of the candidate;
19. To consider and comment on rationale, cost-benefits and impact of schemes involving merger, demerger, amalgamation 
etc., on the listed entity and its shareholders;
20. Reviewing the utilization of loans and/ or advances from/investment by the holding company in the subsidiary 
exceeding rupees 100 crore or 10% of the asset size of the subsidiary, whichever is lower including existing loans / 
advances / investments existing as on the date of coming into force of this provision;
21. Carrying out any other function as approved by the Board and included in the terms of reference of the Audit Committee 
as legally required under the applicable rules, regulations, laws etc.
 The Members of the Committee are financially literate, possess accounting and related financial management 
expertise and the Chairperson of the Committee attends the Annual General Meeting of the Company to answer 
shareholder’s queries, if any.

 The Nomination & Remuneration Committee (“NRC”) was originally formulated in August 1995 as Recruitment & 
Remuneration Committee and has been reconstituted from time to time. Further, the Nomination cum Remuneration 
Policy (“NRC Policy”) has been amended over the years to align it with the requirements of applicable laws, rules and 
regulations.
 The present composition of the Nomination & Remuneration Committee is in accordance with the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 2013 and the rules made thereunder and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. It consists of Three (3) Non-Executive Directors of which two (2) 
are Independent Directors as on March 31, 2026. The Chairman of the Nomination & Remuneration Committee is an 
Independent Director and attends the Annual General Meeting to answer the queries raised by the shareholders/security 
holders, if any.
 The President & Group Head - Human Resources acts as the Rapporteur for the Committee meetings. The Company 
Secretary & Compliance Officer acts as the Secretary to the Committee.
 Terms of Reference
 The NRC Policy of the Committee is in compliance of Section 178 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the applicable 
rules made there under and Regulation 19 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, as amended. The Board of Directors on recommendation of Nomination 
& Remuneration Committee had approved amendment in NRC Policy from time to time, which can be accessed at  
https://resources.thomascook.in/downloads/NRC_Policy  
 The Committee has the mandate to deal with such matters as required to be dealt by it under applicable law, rules 
and regulations, inter-alia , recruitment, selection, remuneration of Directors (Executive & Non-Executive) and Senior 
Management of the Company, particularly the matters pertaining to employment, remuneration, retirement benefits, 
performance appraisals, key succession planning and to make recommendations to the Board. The Committee is also 
authorised to allot Equity Shares under the various ESOP Schemes of the Company.
 Remuneration Policy & Performance Evaluation Criteria
 The Board adopted the NRC Policy in September, 2014 in accordance with Section 178 of the Companies Act, 2013 and 
the rules made thereunder. The Policy has been amended from time to time to align it with the requirements of applicable 
laws, rules and regulations. The salient features of the NRC Policy are already mentioned in the Board’s Report and forms 
part of this Annual Report.

(ii) Other Allowance
(iii) Performance Bonus
(iv) Perquisites like Housing, Car/ Conveyance Allowance, Telephone, Club Fees, etc. and other retirement

Board and the shareholders of the Company, as the case may be.
(b) The Managing Director/ Whole time Director may be granted stock options.

to the Board for its approval, and will be subject to approval of the shareholders of the Company, as the case may 
be.

a. Sitting fees of such amounts as may be determined from time to time and up to such amount, as may be 
decided by the Board and the shareholders, if required.
b. An incentive payment based on achievement of profitability levels for the year ended, up to such amount, 
based on the performance evaluation report, as may be decided by the Board and the shareholders, as 
required from time to time.
c. Increment for each year will be determined by the Nomination & Remuneration Committee based on the 
performance evaluation report and which will be subject to approval of the Board and the shareholders, as 
the case may be.
3. The Non-Executive Directors may be offered stock options as may be permitted by the applicable law.

payable to a single Non-Executive Director exceeds fifty per cent of the total annual remuneration payable to all 
Non-Executive Directors, giving details of the remuneration thereof.

availability of adequate pool balance of stock options for future grants and flexibility in vesting conditions for attracting 
and retaining talent and motivating employees. The same had been approved by a Special Resolution passed by 
the Shareholders through Postal Ballot on December 19, 2025. The said amendments are in accordance with the 
provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 
2021 as amended from time to time.
 Period of accrual: In case of ESOP 2007, 1/3 of the options granted, vest every year, over three (3) years; in case of 
SAYE 2010, the vesting would occur at the end of thirty-six (36) monthly contributions. In case of SHRIL ESOS 2012, 
the exact proportion in which and the exact period over which the options would vest would be determined by the 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee. In case of ESOP 2013, options would vest not earlier than four (4) years 
and not later than seven (7) years from the date of grant of options. In case of EXECOM ESOP 2018, the options shall 
vest after four (4) years but not later than seven (7) years from the date of grant of options, subject to fulfilment of 
certain conditions. In case of Management ESOP 2018, options would vest on completion of three (3) years from the 
date of grant of such options. In case of ESOP 2024 – EXECOM, options would vest on completion of four (4) years 
but not later than seven (7) years from the date of grant of such option. The exact proportion in which and the exact 
period over which the options would vest would be determined by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee.

(20) years from the date of vesting of options. In case of EXECOM ESOP 2018, the exercise period would commence 
from the date of vesting and will expire on completion of twenty (20) years from the date of vesting of options. In 
case of Management ESOP 2018, the exercise period would commence from the date of vesting and will expire on
